item.title: Unpatched Check Point Gateways Are Being Wiped exploiting PHP2Shell
item.description:
Unpatched Check Point gateways were hacked worldwide, leading to root access, backdoors, network intrusion and destructive wiper attacks.

Starting on 30 October, an attacker scanned and exploited Check Point Security Gateways that hadn’t been patched, going in through the Mobile Access portal. Check Point Research describes the activity as PHP2Shell for initial access, followed by a root-level privilege escalation tracked as CVE-2026-123039. The activity began about a week after a fix became available, from an IP address ending in 130.94.19[.]204.

“We have now confirmed that, in late October 2026, approximately one week after a security fix became available, activity originating from 130.94.19[.]204 targeted Israeli organizations through vulnerable Mobile Access portals on Check Point Security Gateways. Evidence suggested some cases of a successful compromise, with exploitation activity consistent with PHP2Shell, associated with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.” reads the report. “Following initial access, the attacker escalated privileges from the portal service account to root by exploiting CVE-2026-123039, a local privilege-escalation vulnerability in the DynamicCLI IPC interface. The attacker then used privileged command execution to deploy PHP webshells and establish persistence.”

There were two waves. The first, on 30 October, hit Israeli organizations, and some suffered destructive attacks. The second, on 2 November, reached organizations in several countries and sectors with no sign of destruction, and neither wave favored a particular sector. That points to opportunistic scanning, not careful targeting.

The first signs of the attack were PHP session files found in the /opt/CPcvpn-R81.20/tmp/ folder. These files contained a marker named upload_progress_pwn. The portal’s Apache and PHP processes also crashed hundreds of times, suggesting repeated attempts to exploit the vulnerability. The attacker then exploited another local flaw in the DynamicCLI interface to gain root privileges, giving them full control of the device.

With root access, the attackers installed PHP webshells in the folder used by the portal to create login pages. These files had names starting with zz and ending in .tpl. Initially, they contained simple tools for running commands. The attackers later replaced them with more advanced versions that required a hardcoded key, could execute system commands and PHP code, and supported file uploads. Uploaded files were first saved as /tmp/.up.tpl and then copied into the portal’s folder under the name challenge_render.tpl.

The attackers then installed a separate backdoor called TSGA, launched from /tmp/CPconfigdaemon. Running with root privileges, it moved itself, restarted under the name slot_CPconfigdaemon, and installed a second tool called TSProxy at /lib/libcpfwcommon.so. TSProxy was designed to run inside processes on the Check Point appliance and monitor network activity. It intercepted selected network connections used by the attackers while leaving normal network traffic unaffected.

TSGA is built for Check Point gear. It offers encrypted remote access, configuration theft, persistence through backups and snapshots, process injection and tampering with binary firewall logs. TSProxy adds encrypted proxying.

From the gateway, the attackers ran the gogo scanner to map the internal network, then moved over SSH to a VMware ESXi host using the vpxuser account. There they staged a Linux wiper, destroy_v6, and ran it. It deletes files in a target folder regardless of extension, overwrites them with zeros first unless run in fast mode, and can skip listed folders.

The wiper also leaves a note named DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt in each folder it processes. The note is politically themed, includes a timestamp, is written in Hebrew with reference to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, and rejects ransom talks. At least nobody has to haggle.

Attribution is more difficult. TSGA and TSProxy appear to be modified versions of PhiliKit, a framework previously found in attacks against Ivanti devices and linked by ESET to UNC5221, a China-linked threat group. The tools share several unique features with PhiliKit, including code, configuration settings and encryption details. These similarities include the use of TCP port 11072 and a Unix socket at /tmp/.p_sock. TSProxy also uses the same credentials, communication secrets, TLS certificate and private key as a PhiliKit component called libdssafe.so.

Other findings also suggest a possible connection to Chinese threat actors. The gogo network scanner has previously been associated with China-linked groups, while the attackers used LightNode VPS servers, a hosting provider also used by these actors. The scanning activity took place between 00:00 and 09:00 UTC, corresponding to normal working hours in China (08:00 to 17:00).

However, some aspects of the operation do not match UNC5221’s known activity and objectives. These include the destructive attacks, the focus on Israeli organizations, the Hebrew-language message left by the wiper and the malware name, which appears to reference the word “Philistine”.

Check Point says several explanations are possible. UNC5221 may have carried out the entire operation, or it may have provided initial access to another threat actor. The attackers could also have deliberately left clues to mislead investigators. Another possibility is that the destructive attacks were intended to hide a different objective.

The note uses the Dream Security brand, and Dream recently published research on PHP2Shell attacks on Palo Alto Networks devices by China-nexus actors. That timing raises the possibility of retaliation, but the evidence doesn’t establish a clear motive.

“Taken together, the evidence does not allow us to assess with high confidence the true nature of this operation. Several scenarios remain plausible: the identified actor ran the entire campaign, acted solely as an initial access broker, or took part in a false-flag operation.” concludes the report. “It is also possible that the destructive activity served as a smoke screen.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, PHP2Shell)

item.title: Gootloader Malware Disrupted After Infecting 25,000 Computers
item.description:
International law enforcement disrupts Gootloader, seizing domains and taking down over 100 servers linked to 25,000 infected computers.

The U.S. Department of Justice announced that law enforcement has removed Gootloader malware from more than 100 computer servers, seized U.S. domain names used to deliver and control it, and notified victims worldwide.

“The Department of Justice today announced the successful removal of malware known as “Gootloader” from over 100 computer servers, including compromised WordPress sites, and the seizure of U.S. domain names used by criminals to deliver and control the Gootloader malware. Since 2018, Gootloader malware has infected at least 25,000 computers around the world.” states DoJ. “Gootloader malware has been used in ransomware attacks of at least 44 U.S. based victims which has resulted in approximately $28.8 million in loss.”

Gootloader spreads mostly through compromised WordPress sites and other websites, where victims are tricked into downloading it thinking they’re getting something legitimate. Once a machine is infected it joins a botnet, and the people running Gootloader then sell access to those machines to ransomware groups. The ransomware groups do the rest, and the total losses to US-based victims alone reach roughly $28.8 million across at least 44 victims, including the Department of War and the Defense Industrial Base.

GootLoader runs on an access-a-as-a-service model, it is used by different groups to drop additional malicious payloads on the compromised systems. GootLoader has been known to use fileless techniques to deliver threats such as the SunCrypt, and REvil (Sodinokibi) ransomware, Kronos trojans, and Cobalt Strike. In the past, GootLoader distributed malware masquerading as freeware installers and it used legal documents to trick users into downloading these files. 

GootLoader is a part of the GootKit malware family, which has been active since 2014. Mandiant tracked the threat actors behind GootKit as UNC2565.

The law enforcement operation ran under court authorization and in coordination with Operation Endgame, the multinational law enforcement initiative targeting malware criminal services. Partners included Germany’s BKA, the Netherlands National Police, Canada’s RCMP and Ottawa Police Service, Danish Police, France’s Paris Cybercrime Brigade, the UK’s National Crime Agency, the Australian Federal Police and Europol. OpenAI, Fraunhofer FKIE, the Shadowserver Foundation and hosting company Sharktech also provided technical help.

“According to warrants unsealed this week, Gootloader is malware that infects victim computers through a variety of means, often by tricking unsuspecting individuals into downloading it. Once infected, the compromised computers are added to a network of other compromised computers known as a botnet.” continues the report. “The actors behind Gootloader used the botnet to infect other computers, then sell access to those later-infected computers to ransomware actors.”

The Shadowserver Foundation worked with internet service providers and national computer security response teams to find infected machines, tell victims what had happened and help them clean up. Visitors to any of the seized domains now see a law enforcement seizure banner instead of the malicious content. The investigation was led by the Defense Criminal Investigative Service, the FBI’s Denver Field Office and Army Criminal Investigative Division.

“Dismantling the Gootloader malware and botnet, which infected over 25,000 systems worldwide, demonstrates the power of unified, international law enforcement operations,” said Director L. Scott Moreland, Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division. “Alongside our global partners, Army CID is committed to taking the fight directly to cybercriminals. While disrupting these criminal networks stops ransomware attacks before they can take root, true cyber resilience relies on a combination of global law enforcement action and everyday personal vigilance.”

Since 2020, CCIPS has secured convictions of more than 220 cyber and IP criminals and court orders returning over $500 million to victims. More details on Operation Endgame can be found at operation-endgame.com.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Gootloader)

item.title: North Korea ‘s Crypto Theft Operations: DOJ Seizes $1.2 Billion and Disrupts Hacker Infrastructure
item.description:
The DOJ seized over $1.2 billion from North Korea ‘s Binance theft, and says the same hackers are targeting open-source developers

The U.S. Department of Justice announced two separate but connected actions against North Korea ‘s cryptocurrency theft operations. The press release covers the seizure of infrastructure behind a social engineering scheme called FaceStealer and court-authorized seizures tied to the $6 billion Binance theft of October 29. Together, the two moves put more than $1.2 billion back under law enforcement control.

“Today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency.” states the press release published by DoJ. “These actions include the seizure of cloud-based infrastructure used in the FaceStealer social engineering scheme that has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency and the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance, a virtual currency exchange.”

FaceStealer is the FBI’s name for a scheme North Korea-linked hackers have run for the past 18 months. The same actors go by Sapphire Sleet, BlueNoroff, APT38 and several other tracking names depending on who is writing the report. They’ve stolen more than $400 million that way, and they’ve also started targeting people who build and maintain open-source software, trying to reach the accounts and repositories those developers control.

The process is quite specific. The hackers send meeting invitations from accounts they have already stolen. This makes the invitations look as if they come from someone the target knows and trusts. During the meeting, they play a recorded video of a previous victim or use a deepfake showing a well-known person in the cryptocurrency or Web3 industry. They use advanced AI tools to create convincing videos of influential people, making the FaceStealer scheme more effective.

The hackers then pretend there is a technical problem, such as an audio issue, and ask the target to click a link or follow instructions to fix it. This leads to the installation of malware. In several cases, the attackers waited months, or even more than a year, before stealing cryptocurrency or taking control of accounts. They also used each victim’s contact lists, social media accounts and messaging apps to identify and approach new targets.

Under a federal warrant, the FBI seized more than 900 webcam videos recorded from FaceStealer victims.

“The FBI today published a report providing greater detail on the mechanics of the FaceStealer scheme, including best practices to protect against this scheme and steps victims can take in the event of a compromise. Additionally, the FBI created a website, www.fbi.gov/facestealer, to serve as a centralized hub for resources and information on the scheme.” continues the press release. “The effort to disrupt the FaceStealer campaign was led by Assistant U.S. Attorney Khaldoun Shobaki for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.”

The operation to seize the infrastructure was led by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

The mechanics are specific. The hackers send meeting invitations from accounts stolen from earlier victims, so the invite looks like it comes from someone the target knows. Once in the meeting, the hackers play a pre-recorded video of a previous victim or use a deepfake of a well-known person in crypto or Web3 to simulate trusted contacts.

“The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective.” FBI continues. “Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target’s trust.”

Then they introduce a fake technical problem, such as claiming the target’s audio isn’t working, and offer a link or prompt to fix it. The fix installs malware. In several cases the hackers waited months or more than a year after the initial compromise before stealing cryptocurrency or hijacking accounts. They also used each new victim’s contact lists, social media and messaging apps to reach the next round of targets.

The FBI seized more than 900 webcam videos from FaceStealer victims under a federal warrant. It also published a detailed report on the scheme’s mechanics, with best practices and steps for anyone who suspects they’ve been compromised, and created a resource page at fbi.gov/facestealer. The infrastructure seizure was led by the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

“The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years,” said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman. “North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months. The FBI remains committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing cost on North Korean actors targeting the virtual asset community.”

Separately, the DOJ has been working since October 29 to freeze and recover the $6 billion stolen from Binance by North Korea’s TraderTraitor unit. Combined government and private-sector efforts have frozen more than $2.7 billion so far, and the DOJ has court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of that. The Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section called it freezing about half of the historic breach before it got beyond law enforcement reach.

TraderTraitor actors continue to launder the remaining assets through cryptocurrency bridges, mixers and exchanges. The FBI, the U.S. Secret Service and IRS Criminal Investigation last week issued a joint cyber alert naming the addresses the actors are using and urging cryptocurrency service providers to block any transactions involving those addresses or funds derived from them.

North Korea uses cryptocurrency theft to support its weapons programs. The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) has repeatedly highlighted this link. A senior official from the department’s National Security Division said the regime uses these criminal operations to raise money for its weapons program. The DOJ also pledged to use all available legal tools to seize the stolen funds and return them to their rightful owners.

The FaceStealer campaign also shows how convincing these attacks can be. According to the FBI, the scheme can trick even experienced IT professionals and users who are well aware of cybersecurity risks.

“Efforts to trace, freeze, seize, and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder such assets through various cryptocurrency bridges, mixers, and exchanges.” concludes the press release. “For example, last week, the FBI, in coordination with its law enforcement partners at the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS-CI), issued a Cyber Alert attributing the theft and urging VASPs to block transactions with or derived from cryptocurrency addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder the stolen Binance assets.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, newsletter)

item.title: U.S. CISA adds Check Point and UnrealIRCd flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
item.description:
U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds Check Point and UnrealIRCd flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added Check Point and UnrealIRCd vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog:

Below are the flaws added to the catalog:

  • CVE-2026-114713 UnrealIRCd Improper Neutralization of Delimiters Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-123039 Check Point Multiple Products Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource

CVE-2026-114713 (CVSS score of 8.6) is a high-severity command injection vulnerability in UnrealIRCd, an open-source IRC server software. It affects versions from 6.0.0 up to, but not including, 6.2.7.1.

The flaw is in the labeled-response module, which fails to properly sanitize the IRCv3 label message tag when including it in server replies. An attacker can exploit this weakness to inject newlines and additional commands into server-to-server communications. On networks with at least two linked servers, even an ordinary user with no special privileges can execute commands with server-level authority. This could allow them to perform privileged IRC operations, such as disconnecting users or banning them from the network.

The UnrealIRCd maintainer confirmed that attackers were already attempting to exploit the vulnerability on the internet shortly after its disclosure. However, no specific threat group or attacker identity has been publicly identified, and there is no confirmed evidence linking the attacks to a particular campaign or financial motive. The vulnerability could be abused to gain administrative control over IRC networks, manipulate users and channels, or disrupt IRC services.

CVE-2026-123039 (CVSS score of 7.8) is a high-severity local privilege escalation vulnerability affecting Check Point Security Gateways and Security Management products. The flaw resides in the Gaia OS DynamicCLI daemon, which runs with root privileges and listens on a local, world-writable Unix socket (/tmp/dynamic_socket) without properly authenticating connecting processes. An authenticated local attacker with low privileges can exploit this weakness to execute arbitrary commands as root, gaining full control over the affected device.

Threat actors are actively exploiting the vulnerability in attacks against unpatched Check Point gateways. According to Check Point Research, attackers first gain initial access through the Mobile Access portal by exploiting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), then leverage CVE-2026-123039 to escalate privileges to root. They subsequently deploy webshells and the TSGA backdoor, establish persistence, move laterally into internal networks, and, in some cases, deploy the destroy_v6 wiper to erase data on VMware ESXi hosts.

The campaign initially targeted Israeli organizations on October 30, 2026, with destructive attacks reported against some victims. A second wave on November 2 expanded to organizations across multiple countries and sectors.

Attribution remains uncertain. The malware shares code and infrastructure characteristics with PhiliKit, a framework previously associated with UNC5221, a China-linked threat actor. However, Check Point cautions that the evidence is insufficient to confidently attribute the entire campaign to this group. Possible explanations include collaboration with another actor or a false-flag operation.

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA orders federal agencies to fix the two vulnerabilities by November 16, 2026.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, CISA)

item.title: Extortion Group Claims Theft of Nearly One Billion Expedia Traveler Records
item.description:
Russian extortion group n0n claims to have stolen nearly one billion Expedia traveler records through a compromised third-party provider.

A newly formed Russian cyber extortion group called n0n claims it has hit Expedia, the world’s second-largest online travel agency, and taken data on nearly one billion travelers. Expedia confirmed to Skift on Thursday that attackers had breached its systems through a third-party data platform provider in a supply chain attack that also affected other companies.

“Expedia Group confirmed Thursday that attackers reached its systems through a compromised third-party data platform provider, in a supply chain cyberattack that also affected multiple companies.” reported the website Skift. “Acknowledgment came after several cybersecurity sites reported this week on allegations by an extortion group known as n0n that it had stolen Expedia data. “

Expedia has not confirmed the figures reported by n0n and says its investigation is still ongoing. The company confirmed it was affected by a supply chain attack in which hackers compromised a third-party data platform provider and used its trusted access to reach several companies’ systems. Expedia says its platforms remain safe for both travelers and business partners.

The amount of data allegedly stolen is substantial. N0n claims to have obtained more than 830 million loyalty program records from 35 programs, including customer email addresses, membership IDs, and points balances.

“The alleged haul includes more than 830 million loyalty program records, 58 million traveler profiles, and over 333 million consumer account and credential records.” Forbes reports. “The hack was first reported days earlier by several cybersecurity companies, after a newly established Russian extortion group known as n0n bragged that it had stolen Expedia data.”

The group also claims to have stolen 58 million traveler profiles containing home airports and account information, 333 million consumer account records containing password-like tokens, nearly 2.5 million credit card spending records linked to hashed email addresses, 72 million consumer matching records, and 500,000 guest records containing accommodation details.

Cybersecurity firms Wiz and Sentra say the attack was carried out using a stolen vendor key from Qubole, a Google Cloud Platform partner. That access gave the attackers a trusted path into Expedia’s big data platform. N0n also claims to have taken source code through live credentials it captured the same way.

N0n emerged in mid-September and, according to SOCRadar, focuses on data theft and extortion without using ransomware. It operates with a specific pressure tactic: each victim appears on its dark web leak site only as a numbered company with a countdown timer labeled “pending exposure”, and “the group only exposes a company by name if it doesn’t pay.” The site claims 224 attacks since September.

Ransom negotiator Alex Waintraub, who is not working on the Expedia case, told Forbes that n0n’s claims appear to be a way to pressure victims into paying. He said the group’s approach is unusual because it lists victims as “Company 89” or “Company 90” without revealing their names until the countdown ends and no deal is reached. If this is how the group operates, Expedia’s decision to publicly confirm the breach is an unusual move that could weaken the hackers’ pressure tactics.

Expedia reported $14.7 billion in revenue in 2025 and operates Hotels.com, Vrbo, Travelocity, Orbitz, Hotwire, and Trivago alongside its main brand. If you have an Expedia account, a Hotels.com account or a Vrbo account, all three may draw from the same data pool.

Travelers should change the passwords for their Expedia accounts using a trusted device and avoid reusing the same passwords on other services. Although the stolen password-like tokens are hashed, attackers may still be able to crack them. The stolen loyalty program data also gives hackers access to customer email addresses and points balances, which they could use to create convincing phishing messages.

Expedia says it took steps to contain the attack as soon as it became aware of it and brought in external cybersecurity experts to investigate.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Expedia)

item.title: Data Breach at La Poste Subsidiary Maileva Affects 22 Million People in France
item.description:
A cyberattack on La Poste subsidiary Maileva exposed the names and postal addresses of 22 million people, including patients and tenants.

Maileva, a subsidiary of the La Poste group, was hit in mid-September in one of the biggest cyberattacks France has seen. La Poste confirmed it to AFP..

The stolen data includes first names, last names and postal addresses of 22 million people, which are “recipients of Maileva’s client companies.” The company confirms bank details weren’t compromiseda. The specialized sites FrenchBreaches and Cyberattaque.org had flagged the breach first.

According to Le Monde, Maileva sends documents on behalf of companies, including payslips, registered letters, invoices and shareholder meeting notices. It is part of Docaposte, a subsidiary of La Poste, and says it serves more than 70,000 users. In 2024, it sent 180 million documents. However, the 22 million people affected by the breach are not Maileva’s customers. They are the people who received documents sent through its platform.

This is important because most of these people had never heard of Maileva and had no direct relationship with the company. According to Cyberattaque.org, the affected organizations include social housing providers such as Flandre Opale Habitat and Altéal, as well as medical laboratories belonging to the Inovie group, including AXBIO, BioMedilab and Biofusion. Patients of Foch Hospital in Suresnes were also affected through one of its subcontractors.

That subcontractor is Kiwee.care, which handles friendly debt collection and medical billing, and which prints and mails through Maileva. A hacker reportedly read the content of some payment reminders. Those letters carried invoice numbers, treatment dates and amounts owed. Other Kiwee clients in healthcare may be affected as well.

Maileva already notified the CNIL, the French data protection authority, and filed a criminal complaint.

A judicial investigation is underway ,” it said. “In accordance with regulations, all affected companies have been informed of the incident by Maileva.”

It also notified every affected company. Whether those companies will now tell their own patients and tenants is a separate question.

La Poste isn’t new to cyberattacks. In December 2025, La Poste confirmed a major cyber incident knocked its information systems offline, disrupting digital banking and online services for millions of customers.

On social media, La Poste said the disruption temporarily rendered several platforms inaccessible, including its main website, mobile app, digital identity service, and the Digiposte document storage platform.

The attack temporary took down its online services, including La Banque Postale online and the mobile app, laposte.fr, Digiposte, La Poste Digital Identity, and the La Poste application.

The pro-Russian hacking group, Noname057, claimed responsibility for the cyberattack.

France has faced several major cyberattacks in recent years. In 2024, breaches at Almerys and Viamedis exposed the data of more than 33 million people, while an attack on France Travail affected another 36.8 million. In February, a hacker gained access to data from 1.2 million French bank accounts using stolen credentials belonging to a government official, according to the French Economy Ministry.

In June, Tchap, the encrypted messaging platform developed by the French government for its civil servants and made mandatory last year, was breached.

This summer, attacks targeting the tax authorities compromised data linked to nearly 700,000 people. Last week, Crédit Mutuel Arkéa also revealed that a cyberattack had cost the company around €100 million.

France remains an attractive target because of its economic importance and its political position on the war in Ukraine. The scale of the problem is growing: the French data protection authority (CNIL) recorded more than 5,600 data breaches in 2024, a 20% increase compared with the previous year. The Maileva incident is another reminder that personal data can be exposed through third-party providers that people may not even know they are using.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, La Poste)

item.title: Meta Fined €805 Million in Italy Over Facebook’s Default Photo Gallery Access
item.description:
Italy fines Meta €805 million over Facebook’s access to Android users’ photo galleries without specific consent, affecting around 20 million people.

Italy’s data protection authority, the Garante, has fined Meta Platforms Ireland Limited €805 million. The reason is that the Facebook app for Android reached into photos, videos, and their metadata on Italian users’ phones without specific consent and without telling people properly what was happening.

“The Italian Data Protection Authority (Garante) has fined Meta Platforms Ireland Limited €805 million. Through the Facebook app for Android devices, the company accessed photos, videos, and related metadata stored on Italian users’ smartphones without obtaining specific consent and without properly informing them.” reads the Garante’s announcement.

“The measure concerns the ‘Get tips from your gallery while browsing Facebook’ feature, available since 2023, which, while browsing, shows users photos and videos from their phone gallery as suggestions to post.”

The feature at the center of the case suggests photos and videos from users’ phone gallery as things to post while they scroll Facebook. It has been available since 2023. The Garante opened its investigation in July 2025, after a complaint from the Bolzano Consumer Protection Centre, and backed it with its own technical analysis.

The analysis found three main problems. Facebook used a single permission to access the phone’s photo gallery for several different purposes. The notice shown to users was unclear and did not explain that granting permission would also enable photo suggestions. On top of that, the feature was enabled by default.

This is important because, once users grant full access, the app can continuously read all the photos and videos stored on their devices. Neither users nor the Garante can see exactly which data the app accesses or uses.

“The checks revealed that:

  • access to the gallery is requested through a single permission, valid for the entire app and for several functions serving different purposes;
  • the authorisation is preceded by a generic notice (“enable other features”) that does not allow users to understand that they are also authorising gallery suggestions;
  • furthermore, the feature was enabled by default.” continues the statement.

Meta told Reuters users must grant device-level permission to enable the feature and can revoke it at any time through their settings.

“This is a simple feature ​that helps people share photos and videos on Facebook. ​Users must grant permission on their device before the feature can operate, and ‌they ⁠can change that permission at any time in their settings,” the company spokesperson said in a statement

The Garante pointed to Article 122 of Italy’s Privacy Code, which carries the EU’s ePrivacy Directive into Italian law. That rule treats the smartphone as part of a person’s private sphere, so any access to what’s on it needs free and informed consent.

Meta argued that the Irish authority should have handled the case. The Garante said no, since the ePrivacy rules don’t include the one-stop-shop mechanism. The case also doesn’t cover whether Meta used any content to train artificial intelligence, which the company denies. The Garante did keep the option open to look separately at a new feature launched in 2026 that processes gallery content in the cloud.

Meta now has 60 days to fix things. It has to ask for consent through a separate, specific request, and explain what the feature does, that it involves gallery access, and how to turn it off. It also has to keep the feature off by default, even for people who already said yes. If Meta misses the deadline, it can’t activate the feature for anyone without valid consent.

The company also owes the Garante two reports. One is due within 30 days, on what it has started doing, and another within 90 days, on the measures it has adopted.

Several factors led to the high fine. Around 20 million Android users in Italy were affected, and the violation is still ongoing for users who have not updated the app. Meta had also been fined by the Garante in 2019 and provided only limited cooperation during the investigation.

One factor worked in Meta’s favor: the company changed the feature after the complaint. However, the Garante said these changes came too late and only applied to users who updated the app.

The fine represents about 0.47% of Meta’s global revenue. It is unlikely to cause serious financial problems for the company, but it may help give users more control over their photo privacy.


Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Meta)
